paras: The lynching of Jack Hillsman was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Knoxville, Georgia, in late July 1900. Hillsman, accused of attempting to assault a planter's 14-year-old daughter, was seized from officers who had brought him back for a preliminary trial, and his body was riddled with bullets. A coroner's jury reported that it could not identify any member of the mob, and the story circulated mainly as a short wire item.

According to a special dispatch from Knoxville, Hillsman, described as 25 years old, was accused of attempting about a week earlier to assault the 14-year-old daughter of James Mitchell, "a well-known planter" of the county. He was arrested on a Thursday and taken to Macon "for safekeeping".

Officers then brought Hillsman back to Knoxville for a preliminary trial. The Manning Times reported that he "was taken from the officers of the law by the lynchers". The mob killed him near the town, and his body was found "riddled with bullets".
A coroner's jury was "unable to find the names of any of the members of the mob". No report of arrests, a grand jury, or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Dawson News, a Georgia weekly, printed the Knoxville special on August 1 under the headline "FOR AN ATTEMPTED ASSAULT. Jack Hillsman Lynched and His Body Filled With Lead." The Caucasian of Clinton, North Carolina, ran the same text the next day as "Negro Lynched in Georgia," with the name set as "Hillleman" and the age as 26. Both versions stated the accusation as established fact and made no comment on the mob.

The Manning Times in South Carolina did not name the victim and headed its brief "For the Usual Crime," a label that presented the lynching as a routine answer to such a charge. The Abbeville Press and Banner carried a one-sentence version a week later, and the Greenville Times in Mississippi described Hillsman as "a negro farm hand".

Outside the South, the case reached readers as a single line in syndicated news digests, set between railroad accidents, fires, and political conventions; a Wisconsin version of the digest called Hillsman "a negro farmhand" as late as August 9. Weeklies in Minnesota, North Dakota, Kentucky, Missouri, and Michigan printed the line "A mob hanged Jack Hillsman (colored) near Knoxville, Ga., for assaulting the young daughter of a planter" or a close variant between August 1 and August 4. No report of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The date of the killing is uncertain: the Caucasian dated the dispatch July 27, while the Manning Times, in its issue of Wednesday, August 1, said the lynching took place "Wednesday night", most likely meaning July 25. The Dawson News said only "last night" in an undated special, and its account of the arrest on "last Thursday" and the return "yesterday" fits the earlier date.
The method also differs: the Knoxville special described only shooting, while the national digest said the mob "hanged" Hillsman.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Hillsman
bases: A mob seized Hillsman, an accused man brought back for a preliminary hearing, and killed him; the reports call it a lynching (A1, A2, A4).

A 'mob' took Hillsman from the officers of the law and shot him to death while he awaited a preliminary trial on an accusation of attempted assault (A1, A2, A4); a mob acting on a criminal accusation meets the standard definition.

Two differently worded wire texts, the Knoxville special (A1, A4, A2) and a separate news-digest line (A3, A17), agree that a mob killed Hillsman near Knoxville, Ga., on a charge of assault, though both probably trace to one Knoxville dispatch and no Georgia local or Black-press report was found.

framing.detail: The Dawson news ran the special under 'FOR AN ATTEMPTED ASSAULT. Jack Hillsman Lynched and His Body Filled With Lead', stating the accusation as fact and making no comment on the mob.
The Manning times headed its unnamed brief 'For the Usual Crime', presenting the lynching as the familiar response to an assault charge.
The Caucasian ran the special under 'Negro Lynched in Georgia'; Northern weeklies reduced it to one line among accidents and fires.

versions.value: On or before July 27 (dateline 'KNOXVILLE, Ga., July 27th')
'Wednesday night' in a paper dated Wednesday, Aug. 1, most likely July 25
'last night', relative to an undated special printed Aug. 1

conflicts.note: The Dawson news text is the same dispatch as the Caucasian's July 27 item, so its 'last night' refers to the dispatch date, not to the Aug. 1 issue; the special's sequence (arrested 'last Thursday', brought back 'yesterday', lynched 'last night') fits a lynching on the night of Wednesday, July 25, as the Manning brief says, but no report gives a calendar date for the killing.
The fuller Knoxville special mentions only shooting; the 'hanged' wording appears only in the one-line national digest condensed from it.
Every other report prints Hillsman; 'Hillleman' is likely a typesetting or OCR variant.

record_check.dossier: Late July, most likely the night of Wednesday, July 25; the dispatch is dated July 27 and no report supports July 31, which appears to come from reading 'last night' against the Aug. 1 issue date.
No county is named in the coverage ('this county').

info: Late July 1900: the Caucasian's dateline is July 27; the Manning times (issue of Wednesday, Aug. 1) says 'Wednesday night'; the Dawson news (Aug. 1) says 'last night' without dating the dispatch.
Jack Hillsman (printed 'Hillleman' in the Caucasian), a Black man aged 25 (Dawson news) or 26 (Caucasian), described as a farm hand in digest lines.
Accused of attempting to assault the 14-year-old daughter of James Mitchell, a planter, about a week before; digest lines say 'assaulting'.

quotes: Jack Hillsman, a negro 25 years of age, was lynched near here last night and his body riddled with bullets by a mob.
He was arrested last Thursday and taken to Macon for safekeeping, but was brought here yesterday for a preliminary trial.
A coroner's jury was unable to find the names of any of the members of the mob.
